KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

A seasonably strong high pressure is forecast to remain in 
place across southern Quebec. This will be the case thru at 
least Thu. High pressure is forecast to continue strengthening 
and building south thru sunrise, with mid level temps warming 
slightly by Thu as the high starts to weaken. So overall I think
this morning has the potential to be the coldest, but not by 
much. Persistence for low temps again tonight may be the best 
way to go, or at least a heavy blend of observed lows with the 
latest guidance.

As a result some areas of frost will be possible into the 
foothills and localized in some of the traditionally cooler 
locations. Frost Advisory remains in effect thru sunrise. Valley
fog will also be possible each mostly clear night where we 
start to radiate.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

By Fri a coastal storm will be organizing and deepening as it 
slowly moves north to a position in the vicinity of the 40N/70W 
benchmark. All guidance forecasts a stall or loop south of 
southern New England before eventually tracking east. This will 
bring a prolonged period of potential impacts to the local 
forecast area. I will try and tackle the impacts in the order of
confidence below:

High surf...A long duration northeast wind with a long fetch 
will allow seas to build thru the first half of the weekend at 
least. Seas building to 10 ft looks likely, but significant wave
heights of 15 to 20 ft are not out of the question if the 
closer/stronger tracks are realized. Despite the poor weather if
that occurs, a High Surf Advisory may still be needed to 
highlight the dangers of large, nearshore breaking waves.

Winds...The strong pressure gradient forecast to set up between
the coastal storm and retreating high pressure. Northeast winds
also tend to keep a fairly well mixed boundary layer thanks to 
cold advection. So I anticipate it will be gusty regardless of 
storm track. Even the weaker guidance at this time is 
forecasting 24 to 48 hours of 30 to 35 mph gusts along the 
coast, especially from Casco Bay southward. As the low level 
cold conveyor belt reaches its strongest Sat into Sun, gusts 
could be even higher than that if the storm really tucks in 
towards Cape Cod. I am not ruling out the necessity for a Wind 
Advisory for parts of the area.

Coastal Flooding...With sustained northeast winds and building 
seas over several days we are primed to maximize the potential 
storm surge by the weekend. Thankfully astronomical tides are 
not peaking until next week, but they will be increasing thru 
the weekend. Some guidance is already indicating that surge 
could be on the order of 2 ft, which would place us near flood 
stage especially Sat night and Sun midday. Something to keep a 
close eye on.

Rainfall...This will be most highly dependent on storm track. 
The farther west the center loops and the longer it meanders off
Cape Cod the better chance we have at seeing widespread soaking
rains. The ECMWF Ens is much more bullish on the west/wetter 
storm tracks, with the GEFS showing plenty of misses in the mix 
still. However both ensemble systems have chance of greater than
2 inches of total QPF between 40 and 60 percent from Portland 
south thru the weekend. The only thing holding me back from 
going with categorical PoP is the uncertainty in timing, as rain
may be most likely anywhere between Sat and Mon depending on 
which model system or ensemble member you look at. QPF will drop
off rather quickly to the northwest of the storm, so much of 
the mtns northward are still looking relatively dry thru the 
event. Given the relative strength of the storm system and the 
lingering warm season moisture/SST profile I am wary that 
dynamics could squeeze out some significant rain even locally if
the track plays out just right. So while right now the forecast
is for a manageable soaking rain, I have my eye on the coastal 
areas south of Cape Elizabeth to the Mass border with a 
reasonable worst case scenario (~10 percent) approaching 4 
inches.
